name: Yellowish Citrine
lede: Yellowish Citrine is a yellowish shade of [[citrine|citrine]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Yellowish Citrine joins the modifier *yellowish* to the base color [[citrine]], named for the citrine quartz [1][4]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XVI, hue 23-single-prime, sets it at lightness 65 with a high chroma of 45[1][4]. The ISCC-NBS system calls the matching block, 103, 'dark greenish yellow,' a Delta-E of 4.5 from Ridgway's point [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[pyrite-yellow]] and [[tennis]], at 4.4 and 4.5 ΔE [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 2.07% of 23,781 paintings, 493 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 359 of them [3]. That ranks it more common than 79% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 2.6% of that century's 1,674 paintings, 1.8 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, by lightness rank, in 64% of its 359 appearances[3]. Georges Seurat is its most devoted painter, using it in 8 of his 41 works here, 6.6 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a painting from 1236, 676 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from India, 2.6 times the expected rate, 24 of 721 Indian paintings in our archive [3]. It shares canvases with [[spanish-bistre]] and [[antique-bronze]] more often than chance, lifts of 9.7 and 6.7 [3].
